items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-11-01
items.q: He was a friend of me. I can tell anybody because he helped me out a lot.

ctx.x: I'm trying to remember the name of another trumpet player. I'm trying to think of the name of the supposed to be another trumpet player, with both, but I just can't remember his name.

Well, I mean, it might have been a man, you know, but this particular picture, which you see in the magazine, that's, uh, uh, for the carnage. I think some of them men, I had one picture with, uh, old man Jimmy Johnson, Biggs, and I played with him. He lived up there around about a two-door, and it's called the 24th. Well, he went to Georgia, and he played with Don Redmond, Don Edgert, Don Alva's band. And, uh, a young boy was, a young man was called Buddy Collins. He went somewhere to Georgia to beat him up upon…
Didn't you say that Collins was sort of like a friend of the family or something like that?

items.title: George Lewis Interview, 1968-11-01
items.q: when you were playing these last jobs with Buddy Buddy... We had played, uh, Longstoker, 48, two singles, uh, uh, Ernest Milton, myself, this member of it.

ctx.x: No, I mean, now I like to play music, like trombone, they're a singer, they're called a singer. When you get to take a melody, the trombone is not supposed to play. It's a vamp instrument. It's a vamp because it's a vamp instrument. In other words, it's a feeling, a basis of feelings. Feel? Yeah, I mean, in between, you don't have no threats. So you feel for that note, you see? When you become accustomed to that, you're here to become accustomed to just what you think. Most of the bass players are playing that…

One thing you talked about before, it was often the tablecorder run out, so if you could mention it again, you were saying when you were playing these last jobs with Buddy Buddy to see before he died. Can you tell about that? See, I was reading in two books. Two different books I was reading in the book by Sam Chardin and the book by Al Rose. They say that there was some picnic or something in Mandeville or something like that. I don't know what that was. No. I don't know what that was. No. No. No. No. No. No.…

You better, you better, there wasn't no picnic until a child. Third, second, third, fourth of July. Goddamn, look, don't you betcha anymore, yeah? Yeah? You get out there? Yeah. Uh, no, it wasn't, it wasn't no picnic. We had played, uh, Longstoker, 48, two singles, uh, uh, Ernest Milton, myself, this member of it. We had played in two nights, come back every morning. Where were you playing? Empire, down Empire, down below the river on the sides, uh, you know, going towards the mountain river. And, uh, that…
